UniversalNER presents a general recipe for targeted distillation from LLMs, demonstrating how to use ChatGPT to generate instruction-tuning data for NER from unlabeled web text, and conducts instruction-tuning on LLaMA to distill the UniversalNER models (UniNER).

The approach explores targeted distillation where student models are trained using mission-focused instruction tuning for open information extraction, showing that this can maximally replicate LLM's capabilities for the given application class while preserving its generalizability across semantic types and domains.

"Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?" is a paper by Sewon Min, Xinxi Lyu, Ari Holtzman, Mikel Artetxe, Mike Lewis, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, and Luke Zettlemoyer, published in the Proceedings of the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing.

**Key findings from the paper:**

The paper shows that ground truth demonstrations are not actually required for effective in-context learning—replacing labels in demonstrations with random labels barely hurts performance. 

The researchers found that what matters for in-context learning are: (1) the label space and the distribution of the input text specified by the demonstrations, (2) specifying the overall format, and (3) these effects are magnified when meta-training with an in-context learning objective.

## Paper Details

"Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles" by Balaji Lakshminarayanan, Alexander Pritzel, and Charles Blundell was published at NeurIPS in 2017.

## Paper Overview

The paper addresses the challenge of quantifying predictive uncertainty in neural networks, noting that Bayesian neural networks require significant modifications to the training procedure and are computationally expensive compared to standard neural networks.

The authors propose an alternative to Bayesian neural networks that is simple to implement, readily parallelizable, and yields high quality predictive uncertainty estimates.

## Key Results

Through experiments on classification and regression benchmarks, they demonstrate that their method produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates which are as good or better than approximate Bayesian neural networks. The method is also able to express higher uncertainty on unknown classes, unlike existing methods which make overconfident predictions even on unknown classes.

The paper is available through multiple sources including the NeurIPS proceedings and arXiv (paper number 1612.01474).

\section{MBR Decoding and Entity Construction}\label{app:mbr_discussion}

\subsection{Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:construction_mbr}}\label{app:mbr_proof}

We show that under entity-wise independence, the MBR-optimal constructed set with entity-F1 utility is the majority-vote set.
Consider constructing $\hat{y} \subseteq E_\cup$ to maximize expected F1 against the empirical sample distribution:
$\mathbb{E}[\text{F1}(\hat{y}, y')] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{2|\hat{y} \cap y_i|}{|\hat{y}| + |y_i|}$.
Under entity-wise independence, the optimization decomposes into per-entity marginal decisions.
For entity $e$ with empirical frequency $\hat{p}(e) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \mathbf{1}[e \in y_i]$, inclusion increases expected true positives by $\hat{p}(e)$ at a false-positive cost proportional to $1{-}\hat{p}(e)$.
At the F1-optimal threshold, inclusion is beneficial iff $\hat{p}(e) > 1/2$, yielding $\hat{y}_{\text{MBR}} = \{e \in E_\cup : \hat{p}(e) > 1/2\}$.
The independence assumption is approximate but empirically justified by the effectiveness of entity-level voting (\S\ref{sec:selection_method}).

\subsection{Connection to MBR Decoding}\label{app:mbr_connection}

Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here: despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation, selection gains are limited by instance degeneracy, the core of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs, consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
The non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472: 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, and the newly non-tied subset shows a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.

Consider constructing $\hat{y} \subseteq E_\cup$ to maximize expected set-overlap against the empirical sample distribution:
$\mathbb{E}[u(\hat{y}, y')] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} |\hat{y} \cap y_i| = \sum_{e \in \hat{y}} \hat{p}(e)$,
where $\hat{p}(e) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \mathbf{1}[e \in y_i]$.
Under set-overlap utility, each entity $e$ contributes $\hat{p}(e)$ independently to the expected utility.
Inclusion of $e$ is optimal iff its marginal contribution is positive, i.e., $\hat{p}(e) > 0$.
However, when we additionally penalize false positives (as in precision-recall trade-offs), the threshold becomes $1/2$: including entity $e$ increases expected overlap by $\hat{p}(e)$ while incurring a cost of $1{-}\hat{p}(e)$ from non-matching samples, so inclusion is net-positive iff $\hat{p}(e) > 1/2$, yielding $\hat{y}_{\text{MBR}} = \{e \in E_\cup : \hat{p}(e) > 1/2\}$.
With F1 utility, the optimal threshold depends on the full probability vector over $E_\cup$ \cite{dembczynski2011exact}; the $1/2$ threshold is exact for set-overlap and a close approximation for F1 when $|E_\cup|$ is small (typically 5--15 in our experiments).
The independence assumption is approximate but empirically justified by the effectiveness of entity-level voting (\S\ref{sec:selection_method}).
